Use the nonrelativistic Newtonian spacetime $I\times E$, where $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ is an open interval with absolute time $t$ in seconds. Here $E$ is a three-dimensional oriented Euclidean affine space: its translation vectors form an oriented Euclidean vector space, but no origin in $E$ is distinguished. A **Cartesian inertial chart** supplies an orientation-preserving affine isometry $x:E\to\mathbb R^3$ and the absolute-time coordinate. Write $\mathrm{SO}(3)=\{Q\in\mathbb R^{3\times3}:Q^TQ=I_3,\det Q=1\}$. Inertial charts are related by

$$t^*=t+t_0,\qquad x^*=Qx+vt+a,$$

where $t_0$ is a constant time translation in seconds, $Q\in\mathrm{SO}(3)$ is constant, $v\in\mathbb R^3$ is a constant relative velocity in m s$^{-1}$, and $a\in\mathbb R^3$ is a constant spatial translation in metres. A **worldline** is a curve $t\mapsto(t,x(t))$ with $x\in C^2(I,\mathbb R^3)$, parameterized by absolute time; this model imposes no relativistic speed or causal condition. A **rigid observer change** is the more general coordinate change $t^*=t,\ x^*=Q(t)x+c(t)$, with $Q\in C^2(I,\mathrm{SO}(3))$ and $c\in C^2(I,\mathbb R^3)$ in metres; it is not called inertial unless $Q$ is constant and $c$ is affine in time. A frame here means an adapted Cartesian chart, not an observer congruence or a basis field.

Let $B\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ be a bounded open reference body whose boundary is locally the graph of a $C^1$ function, with $B$ lying on one side of each such graph. Identify the reference coordinates with the chosen initial Cartesian chart, and let $U$ be an open neighborhood of $\overline B$. A **material motion** is a map $\chi\in C^2(I\times U,\mathbb R^3)$ such that each $\chi_t=\chi(t,\cdot)$ is a bijection from $U$ onto an open image, has a $C^2$ inverse, and has positive Jacobian determinant; in the initial chart set $\chi(0,a)=a$. The label $a\in U$ and position $x=\chi(t,a)$ are measured in metres. Write

$$F(t,a)=D_a\chi(t,a),\qquad J(t,a)=\det F(t,a)>0,\qquad A(t,x)=\chi_t^{-1}(x),\qquad \Omega_t=\chi_t(B).$$

Here $F$ and $J$ are dimensionless and $A$ has units metres. The material map $\chi$ describes motion of the medium; it is not a change of observer or frame. The Eulerian velocity is the vector field defined by $u(t,\chi(t,a))=\partial_t\chi(t,a)$, measured in m s$^{-1}$. For a differentiable scalar or component field $f$, its material derivative is $D_tf=\partial_tf+u\cdot\nabla f$. Set $L_{ij}=\partial_j u_i$, $D=(L+L^T)/2$, $W=(L-L^T)/2$, $\theta=\operatorname{tr}D=\operatorname{div}u$, and $D_0=D-(\theta/3)I_3$; $L,D,W,\theta,D_0$ have units s$^{-1}$. Define vorticity by

$$\operatorname{curl}u=(\partial_yu_z-\partial_zu_y,\ \partial_zu_x-\partial_xu_z,\ \partial_xu_y-\partial_yu_x),$$

also in s$^{-1}$. In this library, a motion is **material-incompressible** on a region when $\operatorname{div}u=0$ there; **spatially homogeneous density** means $\nabla\rho=0$ there. These are distinct conditions. A **pathline** is a $C^1$ curve $X$ on an interval where the field is defined and the solution exists, satisfying $dX/dt=u(t,X(t))$. A **streamline at time $t_0$** is a $C^1$ integral curve satisfying $dX/ds=u(t_0,X(s))$ for a frozen $t_0$, with curve parameter $s$ measured in seconds. These are different constructions for an unsteady field.

A spatial vector is an element of the Euclidean translation space; its components rotate by $Q$ under a rigid observer change. A spatial second-order tensor is a linear map from that vector space to itself, represented by a $3\times3$ matrix in a Cartesian orthonormal basis; it transforms as $S^*=QSQ^T$. A tensor-valued constitutive response is **objective** when its values at corresponding events satisfy this transformation rule for every $C^2$ rigid observer change. For a stress tensor $\sigma$, use the tension-positive convention in which the traction (force per unit current area) on a surface with outward unit normal $n$ is $\sigma n$. Set $(\operatorname{div}\sigma)_i=\partial_j\sigma_{ij}$; the tensor contraction is $S:T=\sum_{i,j}S_{ij}T_{ij}$. Stress and traction have units Pa $=\mathrm{N\,m^{-2}}=\mathrm{kg\,m^{-1}\,s^{-2}}$.

Within a specified model, a **primitive quantity** is a quantity adopted as input rather than constructed from the other data of that model; a **derived quantity** is assigned by an explicit construction from stated inputs and results. This status is framework-local and is independent of whether its SI unit is base or derived. In the continuum model used on this page, $\rho_0(a)$ is a reference mass-density field in kg m$^{-3}$, $b(t,x)$ is an adopted body-acceleration field in m s$^{-2}$, $e(t,x)$ is specific internal energy (energy per unit mass) in J kg$^{-1}=\mathrm{m^2\,s^{-2}}$, $T(t,x)>0$ is temperature in K, $s(t,x)$ is specific entropy in J kg$^{-1}$ K$^{-1}$, $q(t,x)$ is heat flux (heat-transfer rate per unit area) in W m$^{-2}$, and $r(t,x)$ is specific heat supply (power per unit mass) in W kg$^{-1}$. Their adoption is a physical-model choice, not a consequence of the SI. The current mass density $\rho(t,x)$ means mass per unit current volume and has units kg m$^{-3}$; for a mass-conserving motion, its construction from $\rho_0$ and $\chi$ is established from the stated balance hypotheses in the theorem on this page. A pressure $p$ is a scalar in Pa whose role depends on the selected constitutive branch. The shear and bulk dynamic-viscosity parameters $\mu,\zeta$, when that branch is adopted, have units Pa s $=\mathrm{kg\,m^{-1}\,s^{-1}}$; thermal conductivity $\kappa_T$ has units W m$^{-1}$ K$^{-1}$. The gradient $\nabla$ has units m$^{-1}$. Thus the metre, kilogram, second, and kelvin are SI base units in this dictionary, while density, velocity, acceleration, pressure, energy, power, viscosity, and heat-flux units are derived according to the BIPM SI conventions.

Let $\operatorname{Sym}(3)=\{D\in\mathbb R^{3\times3}:D^T=D\}$, let $I$ be the $3\times3$ identity matrix, and define
$$\operatorname{SO}(3)=\{Q\in\mathbb R^{3\times3}:Q^TQ=I,\ \det Q=1\}.$$
An orthogonal matrix is one with $Q^TQ=I$; define $O(3)$ by this condition without the determinant restriction. For $D\in\operatorname{Sym}(3)$ set $\operatorname{tr}D=\sum_{i=1}^3D_{ii}$. Suppose $L:\operatorname{Sym}(3)\to\operatorname{Sym}(3)$ is real-linear, meaning $L(aD+bE)=aL(D)+bL(E)$ for all $a,b\in\mathbb R$ and $D,E\in\operatorname{Sym}(3)$, and satisfies
$$L(QDQ^T)=QL(D)Q^T\qquad(Q\in\operatorname{SO}(3),\ D\in\operatorname{Sym}(3)).$$
Then there are unique $\lambda,\mu\in\mathbb R$ such that
$$L(D)=2\mu D+\lambda(\operatorname{tr}D)I\qquad(D\in\operatorname{Sym}(3)).$$
Conversely, each map of this form is real-linear and satisfies the displayed equivariance. Linearity and rotational equivariance are hypotheses of this mathematical classification; it does not assert that a material response is linear or isotropic.

Let $I\subset\mathbb R$ be an open time interval and $\Omega\subset I\times\mathbb R^3$ open. A smooth constant-density incompressible Newtonian branch has a constant $\rho_0>0$ in $\mathrm{kg\,m^{-3}}$, a constant dynamic shear viscosity $\mu\ge0$ in $\mathrm{Pa\,s}$, a velocity field $u\in C^2(\Omega,\mathbb R^3)$, and a pressure multiplier $p\in C^1(\Omega,\mathbb R)$. Define $L_{ij}=\partial_{x_j}u_i$, $D=(L+L^T)/2$, and $D_tu=\partial_tu+(u\cdot\nabla)u$. The branch is specified by
$$ \rho=\rho_0,\qquad \operatorname{div}u=0,\qquad \sigma=-pI_3+2\mu D,\qquad \rho_0D_tu=\operatorname{div}\sigma, $$
where $(\operatorname{div}\sigma)_i=\sum_{j=1}^3\partial_{x_j}\sigma_{ij}$. Equivalently, for constant $\mu$, its momentum equation is
$$ \rho_0D_tu+\nabla p=\mu\Delta u,\qquad \Delta u_i=\sum_{j=1}^3\partial_{x_jx_j}u_i. $$
Indeed, $\operatorname{div}(2\mu D)=\mu\Delta u+\mu\nabla(\operatorname{div}u)=\mu\Delta u$. This is the incompressible specialization of the adopted Newtonian closure: $\theta=\operatorname{div}u=0$ implies $D_0=D$, so the bulk-viscosity and Fourier-flux terms do not enter this mechanical equation. The pressure is a constraint multiplier and is not identified with a compressible equation-of-state pressure. Define the kinematic viscosity $\nu=\mu/\rho_0$, in $\mathrm{m^2\,s^{-1}}$. Boundary and initial data are not part of this definition, and the item asserts no solution existence.

$$ x^T\operatorname{sym}K(\xi)x\ge0\quad(x\in\mathbb R^3),\qquad \operatorname{sym}K:=(K+K^T)/2. $$

$$t^*=t+t_0,\qquad x^*=Qx+vt+a,$$

Let $B\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ be a bounded open reference body whose boundary is locally the graph of a $C^1$ function, with $B$ lying on one side of each such graph. Identify the reference coordinates with the chosen initial Cartesian chart, and let $U$ be an open neighborhood of $\overline B$. A **material motion** is a map $\chi\in C^2(I\times U,\mathbb R^3)$ such that each $\chi_t=\chi(t,\cdot)$ is a bijection from $U$ onto an open image, has a $C^2$ inverse, and has positive Jacobian determinant; in the initial chart set $\chi(0,a)=a$. The label $a\in U$ and position $x=\chi(t,a)$ are measured in metres. Write

$$F(t,a)=D_a\chi(t,a),\qquad J(t,a)=\det F(t,a)>0,\qquad A(t,x)=\chi_t^{-1}(x),\qquad \Omega_t=\chi_t(B).$$

The Eulerian velocity is the vector field defined by $u(t,\chi(t,a))=\partial_t\chi(t,a)$, measured in m s$^{-1}$. derivations.claim: Differentiate the entropy formula along a material trajectory. The chain rule gives $D_ts=(c_v/T)D_tT-(R/\rho)D_t\rho$. The continuity equation in [L1] is $D_t\rho+\rho\theta=0$, so $D_t\rho=-\rho\theta$. Hence $\rho T D_ts=\rho c_vD_tT+\rho RT\theta=\rho c_vD_tT+p\theta$.

The local internal-energy equation from [L1] and $\sigma=-pI_3+\tau$ give $\rho D_te=-p\theta+\tau:D-\operatorname{div}q+\rho r$, since $I_3:D=\theta$. With $e=c_vT$, this is the stated full temperature balance.
If $\tau=q=r=0$, the temperature equation gives $D_tT=-(R/c_v)T\theta$. Substitution in the differentiated entropy formula of step 1.1 yields $D_ts=-(R\theta)+(R\theta)=0$.

On a trajectory with entropy value $s_0$, solve the entropy formula for $T/T_{\mathrm{ref}}=\exp((s_0-s_{\mathrm{ref}})/c_v)(\rho/\rho_{\mathrm{ref}})^{R/c_v}$. Using $p=\rho RT$, collect powers of $\rho$ to obtain $p=K(s_0)\rho^{1+R/c_v}$ with the displayed positive $K(s_0)$. $$ \rho c_vD_tT=-p\theta+\tau:D-\operatorname{div}q+\rho r. $$

Let $I\subset\mathbb R$ be a nonempty open time interval and $\Omega\subset I\times\mathbb R^3$ a nonempty open domain for the model fields. Let $e\in C^2(\mathcal U)$ be the local specific-energy relation on an open $\mathcal U\subset(0,\infty)\times\mathbb R$, with state coordinates $(v,s)$, $T=e_s$, and $p=-e_v$; each state partial derivative holds the other coordinate fixed. Fix $(v_b,s_b)\in\mathcal U$ with $T_b>0$ and $e_{ss}(v_b,s_b)>0$, set $\rho_b=1/v_b$, and take a barotropic pressure law $P\in C^1((0,\infty))$ that agrees with $p(1/\rho,s_b)$ on an open density interval $J_\rho\subset(0,\infty)$ containing $\rho_b$, with $(1/\rho,s_b)\in\mathcal U$ for every $\rho\in J_\rho$. This is the fixed-entropy restriction of the adopted local state relation. The smooth barotropic Euler model is linearized about the uniform rest state $(\rho,u)=(\rho_b,0)$. For $C^2$ perturbation fields $\delta\rho:I\times\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb R$ and $w:I\times\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb R^3$, the first variation at $\varepsilon=0$ after $\rho=\rho_b+\varepsilon\delta\rho$, $u=\varepsilon w$ is
$$ \partial_t\delta\rho+\rho_b\operatorname{div}w=0,\qquad \rho_b\partial_tw+P'(\rho_b)\nabla\delta\rho=0,\qquad \partial_{tt}\delta\rho=c_s^2\Delta\delta\rho, \quad c_s^2=P'(\rho_b)=v_b^2e_{vv}(v_b,s_b). $$
The sign of $c_s^2$ is not assumed in the base model. If $c_s^2>0$, define $c_s=\sqrt{c_s^2}$. For every nonzero $k\in\mathbb R^3$, with $\omega=c_s|k|$, the fields
$$ \delta\rho=A\cos(k\cdot x-\omega t),\qquad w=\frac{\omega A}{\rho_b|k|^2}k\cos(k\cdot x-\omega t) $$
solve the first-variation system for every real amplitude $A$. They are exact solutions of the linearized equations, not finite-amplitude approximations with an automatic error or lifespan bound. No empirical value of $c_s$ is asserted.

derivations.claim: Differentiation of the chosen state relation gives $T_b>0$, $e_{ss}=C>0$, and $e_{vv}=-A<0$ at $(v_b,s_b)$. For $P(\rho)=p(1/\rho,s_b)$, the chain rule gives $P'(\rho_b)=v_b^2e_{vv}=-Av_b^2=c_s^2<0$.

The derivatives of the stated mode are $\partial_t\delta\rho=\alpha\delta\rho$, $\operatorname{div}w=-\alpha\delta\rho/\rho_b$, $\partial_tw=-\alpha^2a_0k e^{\alpha t}\sin(k\cdot x)/(\rho_b|k|^2)$, and $\nabla\delta\rho=-a_0k e^{\alpha t}\sin(k\cdot x)$. Therefore the continuity equation holds, and the momentum equation holds because $-\alpha^2/|k|^2-c_s^2=0$ by the definition of $\alpha$.

Since $\alpha>0$ and $a_0\ne0$, the density-variation amplitude grows as $e^{\alpha t}$ without bound on $I=\mathbb R$. This smooth first-order solution refutes the stated boundedness claim. It concerns only the linearized mathematical system; it supplies no finite-amplitude solution or empirical material claim.
